speaker: Doctor
text: Hello, I'm Dr. Agent. Can you describe the specific feeding difficulties your 8-month-old son is experiencing, such as vomiting, choking, or poor weight gain? Also, when did you first notice the abdominal distension?

speaker: Patient
text: The baby has been very fussy, feeding less than usual, and the abdomen looks distended. Crying gets worse when the belly is touched.

speaker: Doctor
text: Has your son had any bowel movements or passed gas in the last 24 hours? I also need to know if there has been any vomiting, and if so, what color was it?

speaker: Patient
text: There has not been fever, vomiting, or diarrhea like a stomach infection. The baby was born at 39 weeks without birth complications.

speaker: Doctor
text: Has your son had any bowel movements or passed gas since birth, or was there a significant delay in his first stool? I also need to know if his stools are typically hard and pellet-like when they do occur.

speaker: Patient
text: The baby did not seem to pass stool normally and the belly swelling has become more obvious. Feeding has clearly decreased over the past few days.

speaker: Doctor
text: Given the history of delayed initial stool passage and worsening abdominal distension, I suspect a possible Hirschsprung disease. REQUEST TEST: Abdominal X-Ray. Do you recall if the baby's stools ever had a strong, foul odor or if they were passed only after a digital rectal exam?

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Abdominal X-ray findings show dilated bowel segments with absence of gas in the rectum, suggesting a possible obstruction. Barium Enema findings reveal a transition zone in the distal colon, compatible with Hirschsprung disease. Vital signs show a heart rate of 120 bpm (normal for age) and respiratory rate of 30 breaths/min (normal for age). Abdominal examination notes distension with tympanitic sound in the left lower quadrant and tenderness upon palpation. Blood tests (WBC, Hemoglobin, Platelets) are normal.

speaker: Doctor
text: The imaging and clinical presentation strongly confirm a diagnosis of Hirschsprung disease due to the transition zone and rectal gas absence. DIAGNOSIS READY: Hirschsprung disease.
